notes.title: FRS 105 September 2024: Valuation
notes.keyPoints: Practitioner requirement: When this FRS requires a micro-entity to determine the fair value of an asset or liability, a micro- entity shall use the following methodology to estimate the fair value: (a) The best evidence of fair value is an unadjusted quoted price for an identical or comparable asset or liability in an active market. (b) When an unadjusted quoted price is not available, the price of a recent orderly transaction between market participants for an identical or comparable asset or liability provides evidence of fair value. (c) If neither (a) nor (b) above are available or reliable, the fair value shall be estimated using another valuation technique. The objective of using another valuation technique is to estimate the price at which an orderly transaction to sell an asset or to transfer a liability would take place between market participants at the measurement date.

notes.keyPoints: Practitioner procedure: The assumption that a company is and will continue as a going concern is a fundamental concept in accounting standards and company law that underlies the preparation of financial statements for all UK companies,1 including small companies and micro-entities. Directors of all companies, regardless of size are required to assess the appropriateness of the going concern basis of accounting when preparing the financial statements. As a result, the assessment process for these companies is likely to be simpler than for larger, more complex companies. Nevertheless, it is still important that the assessment is carried out.

notes.heading: Assessment
notes.title: FRS Factsheet 13 The Going Concern Basis of Accounting for Small Companies and Micro entities: Assessment
notes.keyPoints: All companies, including small companies and micro-entities, must assess the appropriateness of the going concern basis of accounting when preparing their financial statements. Financial statements are normally prepared on the assumption that the company is a going concern and will continue in operation for the foreseeable future. The threshold for departing from the going concern basis of accounting is very high, as there are often realistic alternatives to liquidation or cessation of operations. The assessment must take into account all relevant facts and circumstances at the date of approval of the financial statements.

Periodic review 2024 amendments As part of the Periodic Review 2024 amendments, Section 20 Leases was revised to eliminate the distinction between operating leases and finance leases for lessees, and require recognition of more leases on the balance sheet. Cash flows from operating leases would previously have been included within operating activities, whereas cash flows from finance leases would have related to payment of interest (classified either as a financing or an operating cash flow) and repayment of capital (classified as a financing cash flow). Under the new requirements of Section 20, cash flows from leases for which a recognition exemption has been taken are included within operating activities, whereas cash flows from leases recognised on the balance sheet relate to payment of interest (classified either as a financing or an operating cash flow) and repayment of capital (classified as a financing cash flow).

Periodically – notably when inventories are performed and systematically for the closing of each financial year – the current value of these securities must be measured and compared with their net book value (or 'carrying amount,' under IFRS terminology). notes.heading: Changes to the UK Companies Act 2006
notes.title: Changes to the UK Companies Act 2006
notes.keyPoints: Practitioner requirement: In May 2025, the Companies Act 2006 was amended to increase the monetary thresholds used to determine the size of a small or medium-sized company. These changes are effective for financial years beginning on or after 6 April 2025, and cannot be adopted early. It should be noted that there is no change to the size thresholds relating to disclosures in the directors' report for greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and energy efficiency action (Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting or 'SECR'). Changes in directors' report disclosures Disclosures of information in the following areas will no longer be required in the directors' report for companies of all sizes under Schedule 7 to SI 2008/410: the use of financial instruments;

Amendments were also made to the regulations that govern the directors' report disclosure requirements, with some requirements being removed.
